cards.explanation: The answer is with all their heart. Verse 2 says the blessed “…keep His testimonies and seek Him with all their heart.” That's the whole heart, friends. Not the leftover scraps at the bottom of the mixing bowl. The writer wants it all in the dough.

The answer is True. Verse 3 says it straight: “They do no iniquity; they walk in His ways.” The writer is describing the blessed people he just mentioned. Notice the walking and the not doing iniquity are in the very same breath.

The answer is that his ways were committed to keeping God's statutes. Verse 5 says, “Oh, that my ways were committed to keeping Your statutes!” He's talking about his own ways, right after saying God's precepts should be kept diligently. I think you can hear a little ache in that “Oh.” He knows where he wants to land.

The answer is True. Verse 6 says, “Then I would not be ashamed when I consider all Your commandments.” See that little word “then”? It hangs on the wish from verse 5. If his ways were committed to the statutes, he wouldn't be ashamed.

The answer is that he asks God not to utterly forsake him. Verse 8 says, “I will keep Your statutes; do not utterly forsake me.” The promise and the plea come out in one sentence. I think he's the kind of guy who knows he needs help even while he's making the promise. That's an honest way to pray.

The answer is word. Verse 9 asks, “How can a young man keep his way pure?” and answers, “By guarding it according to Your word.” The answer is right there in the same verse. No detours, no ten-step plan.

The answer is so he might not sin against God. Verse 11 says, “I have hidden Your word in my heart that I might not sin against You.” The text gives the reason right there. He tucked it away inside where it stays with him, kind of like a cookie you've hidden in the apron pocket. Except this one is good for him.

The answer is that he asks God to teach him His statutes. Verse 12 says, “Blessed are You, O LORD; teach me Your statutes.” He praises first, then asks to be taught. I think that's the order of someone who knows he still has plenty to learn. And he's okay saying so out loud.

The answer is False. Verse 14 says, “I rejoice in the way of Your testimonies as much as in all riches.” He puts God's testimonies right up there with all riches. He never says he wants the money more. I think he's saying the joy is just as big.

The answer is False. Verse 16 says, “I will delight in Your statutes; I will not forget Your word.” Delight, friends, not a chore. The writer is happy about these statutes. I think that's the real surprise of this psalm.

The answer is so he may live and keep God's word. Verse 17 says, “Deal bountifully with Your servant, that I may live and keep Your word.” The text gives the purpose right there. He wants to live and keep God's word. I think it's like asking for plenty of dough so the batch actually gets baked.

The answer is wondrous things from God's law. Verse 18 says, “Open my eyes that I may see wondrous things from Your law.” That's a request, not a report. He's asking God to open his eyes to the wondrous things from the law. I think that's a humble way to come to the Word.

The answer is commandments. Verse 19 says, “I am a stranger on the earth; do not hide Your commandments from me.” He's a stranger, and he wants the commandments in plain sight. I think a stranger asks for the directions first.
The answer is False. Verse 20 says, “My soul is consumed with longing for Your judgments at all times.” At all times, so not just every now and then. His longing doesn't take a break.

The answer is True. Verse 21 says, “You rebuke the arrogant…” and the writer describes them as the cursed who stray from God's commandments. That's a heavy line, so I'll just let it sit. The writer is speaking directly to God here.

The answer is that he has kept God's testimonies. Verse 22 says, “Remove my scorn and contempt, for I have kept Your testimonies.” The “for” gives the reason. I think he feels the weight of that scorn, and he's bringing it straight to God.

The answer is that he meditates on God's statutes. Verse 23 says, “Though rulers sit and slander me, Your servant meditates on Your statutes.” The rulers sit there talking, and he's thinking on God's statutes. I think that's a calm way to handle it, and honestly I could use some.

The answers are delight and counselors. Verse 24 says, “Your testimonies are indeed my delight; they are my counselors.” He's not just putting up with them, friends, because they make him glad. And he turns to them for counsel. Not a group chat, not a hot take. The testimonies themselves.
